title: Old Testament Survey I: Law and History
summary: Genesis to Esther: creation, the patriarchs, the exodus, the conquest, the kings, the exile and the return.
description: This course walks through the first seventeen books of the Old Testament, from creation to the return from exile. For each section it gives the main events, people and themes, and shows how each step of the story prepares for the coming of Christ, the promised Seed and King.
objectives: Give a clear outline of the Old Testament story from Genesis to Esther
Introduce the main people, places and events of each period
Explain the covenants God made with Noah, Abraham, Israel and David
Show how the history points forward to Christ
outcomes: Place the main Old Testament events in order
Summarise the message of each book from Genesis to Esther
Explain the Abrahamic, Mosaic and Davidic covenants
Describe the causes of the exile and the meaning of the return
Trace the promise of a Saviour through Israel's history

modules.title: Beginnings: Genesis
modules.intro: Genesis is the book of beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood, the nations and the patriarchs.

lessons.title: Creation, fall and flood (Genesis 1-11)
lessons.body:
Genesis opens with God creating all things by His word and making man and woman in His image (Genesis 1:26-27). Adam and Eve disobeyed, and sin and death entered the world (Genesis 3).

Yet God gave the first gospel promise: the seed of the woman would bruise the serpent's head (Genesis 3:15).

Sin spread until God judged the world by the flood, saving Noah and his family in the ark, and making a covenant never again to destroy the earth by water (Genesis 9:11). At Babel, human pride was scattered into nations (Genesis 11).

lessons.title: Abraham and the promise (Genesis 12-25)
lessons.body:
God called Abram from Ur to a land He would show him, promising land, a great nation and blessing: "in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed" (Genesis 12:3).

Abram believed God, "and he counted it to him for righteousness" (Genesis 15:6), the verse Paul uses to explain justification by faith (Romans 4:3). God confirmed His covenant, gave circumcision as its sign, and gave Isaac, the son of promise, in old age.

Abraham's willingness to offer Isaac on Moriah, and God's provision of a ram, foreshadow the Father giving His Son (Genesis 22).

lessons.title: Isaac, Jacob and Joseph (Genesis 25-50)
lessons.body:
The promise passed to Isaac, then to Jacob, whom God renamed Israel. Jacob's twelve sons became the fathers of the twelve tribes.

Joseph, sold by his brothers into Egypt, was raised by God to rule and save many lives in famine. He told his brothers, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Genesis 50:20), a key text on providence.

Genesis ends with Israel's family in Egypt and Jacob's prophecy that the sceptre would not depart from Judah "until Shiloh come" (Genesis 49:10), pointing to the coming King.

The 'first gospel' promise of Genesis 3:15.

The sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his descendants.

In Abraham all families of the earth will be blessed.

Genesis 3:15 gives the first promise of a Saviour.
God's covenant with Abraham promises a people, a land and blessing to the nations.
Through Joseph, God preserves Israel in Egypt; Judah will produce the King.

modules.title: Redemption and Law: Exodus to Deuteronomy
modules.intro: God redeems Israel from Egypt, gives His law at Sinai, dwells among them and leads them to the edge of the promised land.

lessons.title: The exodus
lessons.body:
Israel multiplied in Egypt and was cruelly enslaved. God called Moses at the burning bush, revealing His name, "I AM THAT I AM" (Exodus 3:14).

After ten plagues, the last was the death of the firstborn. Families who killed a lamb and put its blood on their doorposts were passed over: "when I see the blood, I will pass over you" (Exodus 12:13). God then brought Israel through the Red Sea.

The Passover is a clear picture of Christ: "Christ our passover is sacrificed for us" (1 Corinthians 5:7).

lessons.title: Sinai, law and tabernacle
lessons.body:
At Mount Sinai God made a covenant with the redeemed nation and gave the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20). Note the order: God first saved them, then gave the law to shape their life as His people.

He also gave instructions for the tabernacle, a portable tent where His glory dwelt among them (Exodus 40:34). Leviticus explains the priesthood and sacrifices, especially the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), and calls Israel to holiness: "be holy; for I am holy" (Leviticus 11:44).

Hebrews shows that these were shadows fulfilled in Christ (Hebrews 9:11-12).

lessons.title: Wilderness and renewal
lessons.body:
In **Numbers**, Israel refused to enter Canaan through unbelief after the spies' report, and wandered forty years until that generation died (Numbers 14). Yet God provided manna, water and the bronze serpent, which Jesus applied to His cross (John 3:14).

**Deuteronomy** records Moses' final sermons on the plains of Moab, renewing the covenant with the new generation. It contains the Shema, "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and calls Israel to choose life by loving and obeying God (Deuteronomy 30:19-20).

Moses died, and Joshua was appointed to lead.

modules.title: Land and Judges: Joshua, Judges, Ruth
modules.intro: Israel enters the promised land, then falls into cycles of sin and rescue, while Ruth shows God's quiet faithfulness.

lessons.title: Joshua: taking the land
lessons.body:
God told Joshua, "Be strong and of a good courage" and to meditate on His law (Joshua 1:8-9). Israel crossed the Jordan on dry ground, and Jericho fell when they obeyed God's unusual command (Joshua 6).

Rahab, a Canaanite who believed, was spared and later appears in the line of Christ (Joshua 2; Matthew 1:5). Achan's hidden sin brought defeat at Ai (Joshua 7).

The land was divided among the tribes, and Joshua's final challenge still rings: "choose you this day whom ye will serve... as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD" (Joshua 24:15).

lessons.title: Judges: the downward cycle
lessons.body:
After Joshua, a generation arose "which knew not the LORD" (Judges 2:10). Judges follows a repeated cycle: Israel sins, God allows oppression, the people cry out, God raises a judge to deliver them, and there is rest, until they sin again.

The judges include Deborah, Gideon and Samson: flawed people used by God's grace.

The book ends in moral chaos, repeating: "In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25). It shows the need for a righteous king.

lessons.title: Ruth: kindness in dark days
lessons.body:
Set "in the days when the judges ruled" (Ruth 1:1), Ruth tells of a Moabite widow who chose Israel's God: "thy people shall be my people, and thy God my God" (Ruth 1:16).

Boaz, a relative of her late husband, acted as **kinsman-redeemer**, buying back family land and marrying Ruth (Ruth 4:9-10). Their son Obed was the grandfather of King David (Ruth 4:17).

Ruth shows God's providence in ordinary life, His welcome of Gentiles, and a picture of Christ, our Kinsman-Redeemer who took our flesh to redeem us.

A leader God raised to deliver Israel from oppressors.
The pattern of sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance and rest.

texts.teaches: Meditating on God's law day and night brings good success.

Judges shows a cycle of sin and rescue and the need for a righteous king.
Ruth shows God's providence and His welcome of Gentiles.
Boaz the kinsman-redeemer points to Christ.

modules.title: The Kingdom: Samuel, Kings and Chronicles
modules.intro: Israel gets kings: Saul, David and Solomon, then the kingdom divides and declines.

lessons.title: Samuel, Saul and David
lessons.body:
Samuel, born in answer to Hannah's prayer, became prophet and last judge. Israel demanded a king "like all the nations" (1 Samuel 8:5), rejecting God's rule. Saul began well but disobeyed, and God said, "to obey is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22).

God chose David, the shepherd, for "the LORD looketh on the heart" (1 Samuel 16:7). David defeated Goliath, waited patiently for the throne, and made Jerusalem his capital.

In 2 Samuel 7 God promised David an everlasting throne through his offspring, fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David (Luke 1:32-33).

lessons.title: Solomon and the divided kingdom
lessons.body:
Solomon asked for wisdom, built the temple, and the glory of God filled it (1 Kings 3:9; 8:10-11). But his many foreign wives turned his heart to idols (1 Kings 11:4).

After his death the kingdom split (about 930 BC): ten northern tribes formed **Israel** under Jeroboam, who set up golden calves; **Judah** in the south remained under David's line in Jerusalem (1 Kings 12).

Kings are judged by one standard: did they do what was right in God's eyes, like David, or evil?

lessons.title: Prophets, decline and fall
lessons.body:
God sent prophets to call kings and people back. Elijah confronted Ahab and the prophets of Baal on Mount Carmel: "How long halt ye between two opinions?" (1 Kings 18:21). Elisha continued his ministry.

The north never had a godly king. It fell to Assyria in 722 BC (2 Kings 17). Judah had some reforming kings, such as Hezekiah and Josiah, but persisted in idolatry and fell to Babylon in 586 BC, when Jerusalem and the temple were destroyed (2 Kings 25).

**Chronicles** retells this history for the returned exiles, focusing on David's line and the temple.

modules.title: Exile and Return: Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther
modules.intro: God keeps His promise to bring His people home, rebuilds the temple and the walls, and protects them in exile.

lessons.title: Return and rebuilding the temple
lessons.body:
Jeremiah had prophesied seventy years of exile (Jeremiah 29:10). In 539 BC Persia conquered Babylon, and King Cyrus decreed that the Jews could return and rebuild the temple, as Isaiah had foretold by name (Ezra 1:1-4; Isaiah 44:28).

Under Zerubbabel and Jeshua, the exiles laid the foundation. Opposition stopped the work for years, until the prophets Haggai and Zechariah stirred the people, and the second temple was completed in 516 BC (Ezra 6:14-15).

Later, Ezra the scribe came to teach God's law in Israel (Ezra 7:10).

lessons.title: Nehemiah: rebuilding the walls
lessons.body:
Nehemiah, cupbearer to the Persian king, wept and prayed when he heard Jerusalem's walls were broken (Nehemiah 1:4-11). With the king's permission he led the people to rebuild, facing mockery and threats with prayer and watchfulness: "we made our prayer unto our God, and set a watch" (Nehemiah 4:9).

The wall was finished in fifty-two days (Nehemiah 6:15). Ezra read the law to the people, who wept, repented and renewed the covenant (Nehemiah 8-10).

Nehemiah is a model of prayerful, practical leadership.

lessons.title: Esther: God unseen but present
lessons.body:
Esther is set among Jews who remained in Persia. God's name is never mentioned, yet His hand is everywhere. Haman plotted to destroy all Jews; Esther, made queen, risked her life to plead for her people. Mordecai asked her, "who knoweth whether thou art come to the kingdom for such a time as this?" (Esther 4:14).

The king honoured Mordecai, Haman was hanged, and the Jews were delivered. The feast of Purim remembers it (Esther 9).

The Old Testament history closes with God's people back in the land, waiting for the promised King.

The temple rebuilt after the exile and completed in 516 BC.
The governor of David's line who led the first return and temple rebuilding.

The faithful part of God's people whom He preserves through judgement.

short.q: What did God promise Abraham in Genesis 12?
short.model: A land, a great nation of descendants, and that in him all families of the earth would be blessed.

short.q: How does the Passover point to Christ?
short.model: The lamb's blood protected Israel from judgement; Christ our Passover was sacrificed so that judgement passes over those sheltered by His blood.

short.q: Describe the cycle in the book of Judges.
short.model: Israel sinned, God let enemies oppress them, they cried out, God raised a judge to deliver them, and there was rest until they sinned again.

short.q: What did God promise David in 2 Samuel 7, and how was it fulfilled?
short.model: God promised David an everlasting house, throne and kingdom through his offspring, fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Son of David.

short.q: Why did Israel and Judah go into exile?
short.model: Because they persisted in idolatry and sin despite the prophets' warnings, God judged them by sending them into exile.

short.q: What does the book of Esther teach about God?
short.model: Although God is not named, He is at work in His providence, protecting and delivering His people.

assignments.title: The promise through history
assignments.prompt: Trace the promise of a Saviour from Genesis 3:15 through Abraham, Judah and David. For each step, quote the KJV reference, explain what it adds, and show how the New Testament says it is fulfilled in Christ.

assignments.title: Lessons from a leader
assignments.prompt: Choose one leader from this course (Joseph, Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samuel, David, Nehemiah or Esther). Summarise their story, what God did through them, their strengths and failures, and two lessons for Christian leadership today.
